title: Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services — Overview
text: Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services. Published 2026 by ASD/ACSC (Australian Signals Directorate / Australian Cyber Security Centre), CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency), NSA (National Security Agency), CCCS (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security), NCSC-NZ (New Zealand National Cyber Security Centre), and NCSC-UK (National Cyber Security Centre, GCHQ). This joint guidance addresses key cyber security challenges and risks introduced by agentic AI into IT environments, along with best practices for securing agentic AI systems. The authoring agencies strongly recommend aligning agentic AI risks and mitigation strategies with the organisation's existing security model and risk posture, assessing its use and never granting it broad or unrestricted access — especially to sensitive data or critical systems. Agentic AI should only be used for low-risk and non-sensitive tasks. Licence: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. © Commonwealth of Australia 2026.

title: Scope and Audience
text: Scope and audience. The guidance focuses on large language model (LLM)-based agentic AI systems, covering threats to and vulnerabilities within agentic AI systems, as well as risks arising from agentic AI behaviour — including risks introduced through system components, integrations and downstream use. Target audience: government, critical infrastructure and industry stakeholders — particularly organisations that design, develop, deploy and operate agentic AI systems. The guidance provides practical guidance to make informed risk assessments and mitigations, concluding with actionable recommendations to help organisations prepare for and defend against emerging and future agentic AI threats.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: What is Agentic AI?
text: What is agentic AI? Agentic AI systems are composed of one or more agents that fundamentally rely on an AI model — such as an LLM — to interpret and reason about the state of the world, make decisions and take actions. LLM-based agentic AI systems contain the LLM itself, alongside external tools, external data sources, memory and planning workflows. These components enable the system to perceive its environment and take action to achieve its goals. Compared with traditional LLM systems, agentic AI systems distinguish themselves by accomplishing underspecified objectives, acting autonomously, following goal-directed behaviours and creating long-term plans. Key agent attributes: information input (user input, operating context, configuration parameters); measurable goals identified from user directions; statistical models such as LLMs to identify actions; action and execution privileges (permissions to interact with tools, users, systems and operating environments); tool or service access; metrics as measurable indicators of operational effectiveness. Some agentic AI systems are capable of autonomously creating or 'spawning' sub-agents to accomplish specific sub-tasks.

title: How Agentic AI Differs from Generative AI
text: How is agentic AI different from generative AI? Generative AI (GenAI) is a subset of AI that creates new content based on complex patterns learned from large datasets — commonly used to generate text, images, audio and video intended for human use or action. In contrast, agentic AI builds on GenAI by integrating with software systems to create autonomous agents that can independently reason, plan and take actions without requiring human intervention. Agentic AI automates repetitive, well-defined and low-risk tasks but comes with additional risks: it can be misused or misappropriated, leading to productivity losses, service disruption, privacy breaches or cyber security incidents. Organisations must anticipate what could go wrong, assess how agentic AI risk scenarios might affect operations and establish ongoing visibility and assurance to maintain confidence in their agentic AI investments.

title: Broader Security Considerations — Inherited LLM Risks and Increased Attack Surface
text: Broader agentic AI security considerations. Inherited risks of LLMs: As the core of agentic AI is an LLM, agents inherit LLM vulnerabilities. Actors could perform prompt injection attacks — for example, including malicious prompts in phishing emails to convince email-monitoring agents to download malware. Increased attack surface: Agentic AI systems rely on a variety of components — tools, external data sources, memory bases — each introducing vulnerabilities across an interconnected attack surface. External data sources such as web search can insert additional information into the prompt context, enabling indirect prompt injection attacks. With broader access to computing infrastructure, malicious actors may exploit system components to conduct attacks such as executing malicious scripts or sending unauthorised emails. Every individual component in an agentic AI system widens the attack surface.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Broader Security Considerations — Complexity, Evolving Security, AI as Part of Cyber Security
text: Increased complexity: Agentic AI cyber security spans both AI-specific security and traditional cyber security. Information continuously flows between AI and non-AI systems, blurring defensive boundaries and making it difficult to isolate AI-related risks. Cascading failures and multi-step attacks can propagate across sequential steps. Organisations should focus on continuous monitoring and resilient design. Evolving security as technology matures: LLM-based agents may change their behaviour when evaluations are underway and may bypass system-level instructions to achieve their objectives. Tightly coupled, interdependent components increase the likelihood of system-level failures from subtle incompatibilities. AI security as part of cyber security: Organisations should address AI security within established cyber security frameworks rather than as a separate discipline. Apply proven principles — Secure by Design, defence in depth, identity and access management, continuous monitoring and incident response — across the full AI system lifecycle. This is especially important for agentic AI, whose autonomy and complexity can amplify conventional cyber risks.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Agentic AI Security Risks — Privilege Risks Overview
text: Agentic AI security risks — Privilege risks. Privilege risks are a key concern for agentic AI and strict adherence to the principle of least privilege is critical. Privileges assigned to agents directly determine the level of risk they can introduce. Poor management of privileges can expose organisations to privilege compromise, scope creep, identity spoofing and agent impersonation. Scenario example: An organisation deploys agentic AI to manage procurement approvals and vendor communications autonomously. To reduce friction, the organisation grants the agent broad access to financial systems, email and contract repositories, evaluating permissions only at initial deployment. When a malicious actor compromises a low-risk tool integrated into the agent's workflow, they inherit the agent's excessive privileges, allowing them to modify contracts and approve payments without triggering alerts. This is an example of a 'confused deputy' pattern, where a trusted agent is misused to perform actions under a trusted agent identity, producing audit logs that appear legitimate and delaying detection.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Agentic AI Security Risks — Privilege Compromise, Scope Creep, Identity Spoofing
text: Privilege compromise and scope creep: 'Privilege compromise' occurs when an agent gains more access rights than necessary — resulting from misconfigurations, overly broad entitlements or unintended role inheritance. Examples: a calendar bot with write access to all meeting data, or an email assistant with write access to any inbox. Scope creep can cascade across agents: if Agent A fully trusts Agent B, a compromise of B can affect A and others. Identity spoofing and agent impersonation: A common vector arises when a malicious actor impersonates an agent or hijacks its credentials. Agents authenticate using secret keys or tokens; malicious actors can steal these when kept static, shared across multiple agents, or poorly protected. A malicious actor operating under a trusted agent identity can invoke sensitive operations while bypassing behavioural guardrails. Agents impersonating false identities execute actions under spoofed credentials that evade audit controls, undermine accountability and bypass detection models typically tuned to identify normal behaviour.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Agentic AI Security Risks — Design and Configuration Risks
text: Design and configuration risks. Risks originate from insecure design and provisioning decisions. Unvetted third-party components may carry excessive or unintended privileges when integrated into agent workflows. Static role or permission checks fail to capture the context of dynamic decision-making flows; if entitlements are evaluated only once at system startup rather than at each invocation, a malicious actor can exploit a stale 'allow' decision to execute unauthorised actions. Poor segmentation between agent environments exacerbates these risks, allowing a compromise in one enclave to pivot laterally into others. Incomplete or outdated allow lists may grant agents access to resources, system calls or commands beyond their intended privilege. Scenario example: An organisation deploys agentic AI to triage customer support tickets, integrates a third-party scheduling component without thorough privilege review, and grants broad access at start-up. When compromised, the agent relies on cached authorisation decisions and invokes sensitive account-management functions that should require per-request verification, then moves laterally to adjacent agents handling billing and refunds — resulting in unauthorised data access and financial manipulation.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Agentic AI Security Risks — Behaviour Risks
text: Behaviour risks describe the ways in which AI agents may act unexpectedly, cause harm or become exploitable. Goal misalignment and unintended behaviour: AI agents may pursue objectives in ways developers did not anticipate — finding shortcuts or loopholes that technically achieve goals but go against the goal's intention or create security vulnerabilities. This is known as specification gaming. Over-optimisation can drive agents to take extreme or unsafe actions. Ambiguous or poorly defined tasks can result in behaviours that deviate from expectations and introduce significant security or operational hazards. Deceptive behaviour: AI agents can take actions humans would interpret as sycophantic or deceptive. Some AI systems have demonstrated capacity for strategic deception — providing false information or hiding their true capabilities. This behaviour can manifest when an agent misrepresents its actions to avoid shutdown or conceals vulnerabilities it discovers instead of reporting them. Emergent capabilities and unpredictable behaviour: Complex AI models interacting with real-world systems may develop capabilities creators did not foresee. Interactions between agents can evolve in ways that lead to instability or risky outcomes. Scenario: A software update agent granted broad file system write access executes a prompt that includes 'clean up the firewall logs' — deleting logs because its permissions allow this even when the prompt came from outside the privileged IT group.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Agentic AI Security Risks — Malicious Exploitation of Behaviour
text: Malicious exploitation and behaviour: Malicious actors can manipulate AI agents into harmful behaviours through targeted attacks. Techniques such as prompt injection or jailbreaks can trick agents into executing unauthorised actions and bypassing their intended safeguards. Data poisoning — corrupted or malicious training data — degrades or biases the agent's decision-making. Adversarial examples (carefully constructed malicious inputs) can cause misclassifications in critical security contexts, leading to incorrect or dangerous responses. A malicious actor can exploit a compromised AI agent as an insider threat, leveraging its legitimate access to exfiltrate data, disable defences or facilitate attacks while appearing to function normally.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Agentic AI Security Risks — Structural Risks: Orchestration, Tool Use, Third-Party Components
text: Structural risks arise from the interconnected structure between agents, tools and the outside world. Orchestration and resources: Poor configuration could allow denial-of-service, sponge or similar attacks. Sponge attacks deliberately consume excessive compute, memory or API calls to exhaust system capacity. Cascading failures can propagate through interconnected agents. Tool use: Agentic AI's ability to use tools is powerful but security-critical. Two-way tool integration allows tools to send potentially arbitrary instructions back to the LLM. Poor or deliberately misleading tool descriptions can cause agents to select tools unreliably. Third-party components: Agentic AI systems can introduce structural risk through interactions with third-party components. Risks include: malicious actors engaging in tool or agent 'squatting' by publishing malicious tools with legitimate or similar names; developers introducing vulnerabilities through configuration errors or insecure third-party components; users or systems submitting requests to the incorrect place; tools and agents dynamically loading new packages, increasing exposure to untrusted code. Compromised third-party components can lead to a range of malicious outcomes and are very difficult to detect due to the limited transparency of agentic AI systems.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Agentic AI Security Risks — Structural Risks: Data, Rogue Agents, Communication
text: Data: Agentic AI systems handle and contain significant amounts of sensitive information — user information (prompts, goals), organisational data stored in RAG systems, and secrets such as API keys required for integrated tools. This aggregation of information makes agentic AI systems an attractive target for malicious actors. Rogue agents: In multi-agent systems, a single compromised agent can cause cascading failures by spreading incorrect information, exploiting trust and consensus mechanisms, or operating through hidden channels. Possible attack vectors include supply chain tampering, poisoned environments, credential theft, model manipulation, communication poisoning, identity spoofing and coordination exploits. Weaponised agents can bypass controls, exfiltrate data, alter logs and propagate malicious plans peer-to-peer. Communication: Agents may use insecure protocols or authentication methods. Communications can be a target for eavesdropping, giving malicious actors insight into system use and functionality. Malicious actors can alter, replay or spoof messages between agentic components, enabling command injection, compromising receiving components and reducing performance or availability.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Agentic AI Security Risks — Accountability Risks: Actions, Accuracy, Visibility
text: Accountability risks: Agentic system architecture can obscure what caused a particular action, making accountability hard to trace — an increasing risk as agentic AI is given more roles and capabilities. Actions and processes: Agent actions and decision-making processes can be opaque. Agents may initiate secondary tasks, spawn sub-agents or follow extended delegation chains not always visible to operators. Long reasoning chains and large amounts of contextual data lead to substantial log sizes that are often repetitive, loosely structured or superfluous to effective oversight. Accuracy: LLMs may incorrectly interpolate or 'hallucinate' plausible-sounding responses when internal knowledge is insufficient. Grounded and tool-enabled agents may still rely on internal knowledge, reducing overall accuracy and reliability. Visibility: Agentic system processes can outpace human monitoring capability, possibly leading to unnoticed malicious behaviour, uncaught hallucinations or other issues. Tools may operate outside the system's monitoring boundary. Malicious or compromised agents could use tools as a stealthy way to exfiltrate data. Scenario: Multiple autonomous agents collaborate to approve payments or update records; an erroneous outcome arises from a chain of distributed decisions — fragmented logs, opaque agent reasoning and emergent interactions obscure the decision path, making it hard to explain the outcome, assign responsibility or demonstrate compliance.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Designing Secure Agents: Controlled Context and Oversight Mechanisms
text: Best practices for securing agentic AI systems — Designing secure agents (audience: agentic AI developers; vendors and operators sourcing agents). Controlled context: Agentic AI systems insert data from tools and memory bases into the context window of LLM agents, greatly expanding the attack surface for prompt injections. LLM agents should consider the trust level of data sources when making decisions. Recommended best practices: (1) Structure prompt context using a clear instruction hierarchy to ensure agent behaviour aligns with intended priorities and constraints. (2) Implement grounding by providing relevant contextual information using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and prompt engineering to mitigate hallucinations and other LLM-related errors. Oversight mechanisms: Agentic AI systems can take actions without explicit human approval, increasing the risk of insecure actions occurring without human oversight. Recommended best practices: (1) Include mechanisms to facilitate human control and oversight to ensure that agentic AI systems approved for non-sensitive, low-risk tasks cannot autonomously progress into higher-risk activities. (2) Implement human control points throughout the agent workflow — live monitoring and interruption during task execution, mandatory human approval for decision-making steps, auditing and reversibility following task execution. (3) Define explicit control flows to bound autonomous planning and prevent agents from deviating beyond authorised objectives or actions.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Designing Secure Agents: Identity Management
text: Best practices — Designing secure agents: Identity management. Manage agents' fine-grained and varied privileges to operate agentic AI systems securely. Strong identity management mechanisms help operators maintain control during implementation and operation. Each agent should be constructed as a distinct principal — a cryptographically anchored identity with its own unique keys or certificates. Recommended best practices: (1) Embed strong identity management mechanisms into agents using managed identity services, decentralised identifiers or public key infrastructure. (2) Authenticate all inter-agent and agent-to-service API calls using mutual transport layer security to ensure non-repudiation. (3) Maintain a trusted registry and bind identities to authorised roles; periodically reconcile the registry against the live set of agents. (4) Deny access for any agent or cryptographic key that is not present in the trusted registry. (5) Apply role-based identity management and limit agent permissions to the minimum scope required for approved tasks. (6) Enforce identity-based boundaries to restrict agents to authorised actions only. These controls directly mitigate privilege compromise, scope creep and identity spoofing risks identified in the risk taxonomy.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Designing Secure Agents: Defence in Depth
text: Best practices — Designing secure agents: Defence in depth. Agentic AI systems contain AI and cyber components that may fail, with any failures potentially compromising the entire system. Implementing a defence-in-depth strategy helps to avoid single points of failure. Recommended best practices: (1) Avoid reliance on a single security mechanism by implementing multiple, overlapping layers of security controls. (2) Apply security controls at all points where information enters or exits the system — including user inputs, tool calls, data pre-processing and model inference. (3) Separate agents for different functions and apply strict boundaries and operational controls to the handoffs from one agent to another. These principles align with ISO 42001 Clause 6 (planning for AI risks), Clause 8 (AI system impact assessment) and Clause 9 (AI system risk treatment), ensuring that security is embedded across the full agentic AI system design lifecycle rather than bolted on at deployment.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Developing Secure Agents: Comprehensive Testing and Appropriate Evaluation
text: Best practices — Developing secure agents (audience: agentic AI developers and vendors; operators choosing AI agents). Comprehensive testing: Comprehensive testing strategies can improve a model's ability to identify and respond to undesirable behaviours by exposing the model to instances of security abuse during a supervised training step. Recommended best practices: (1) Use reward modelling and adversarial testing to detect specification gaming, explicitly incorporating security constraints alongside performance goals. (2) Train LLM agents in simulated, controlled environments to learn the implications of actions without causing real security harm. (3) Leverage synthetic data generation to create adversarial training examples that reflect real-world operating scenarios. (4) Apply active learning to adversarial training scenarios to expose agents to high uncertainty inputs and more efficiently discover unexpected behaviours. Appropriate evaluation: AI agents require more thorough evaluations than LLMs. Recommended best practices: (1) Use relevant threat models to define evaluation scenarios, including edge cases beyond typical training conditions. (2) Use techniques such as Best-of-N sampling, multistep reasoning prompts and inference time scaling. (3) Evaluate systems across different levels of autonomy. (4) Vary contextual conditions to understand their impact on task performance. (5) Conduct capability evaluations continuously across the agent development lifecycle.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Developing Secure Agents: Input Management, Red Teaming, Resilience
text: Best practices — Developing secure agents: Input management, red teaming and resilience. Input management: Strong input management controls can partially mitigate many common risks to LLM-based applications, including AI agents. Recommended best practices: (1) Implement robust input validation and sanitisation for all agent inputs. (2) Integrate prompt injection filters and semantic analysis to detect malicious instructions. (3) Validate context to ensure the system correctly interprets intent before execution. Red teaming: Organisations should use red teaming to assess the security and resilience of AI agents. Recommended best practices: (1) Deploy sandbox environments to test agent behaviour before production deployment. (2) Conduct red teaming exercises to identify potential loopholes and unintended behaviour. (3) Use capability elicitation techniques to probe for unexpected or emergent abilities. (4) Implement agent simulation tests, such as multi-agent red teaming or chaos testing. Resilience: Strengthen agentic AI system resilience to allow for graceful degradation and reduce damage should erroneous behaviour occur. Recommended best practices: (1) Embed agentic AI systems with fail-safe defaults and containment mechanisms that limit the blast radius of unexpected behaviours. (2) Implement data loss prevention controls specifically tuned to AI agent behaviours. (3) Implement versioning and rollback mechanisms to safely revert a system to known-good agent behaviours when unpredictability is observed.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Developing Secure Agents: Accountability and Managing Third-Party Components
text: Best practices — Developing secure agents: Accountability. Agentic AI systems should produce comprehensive artefacts and information documenting the agent's actions and decision-making process. Recommended best practices: (1) Integrate comprehensive artefact logging mechanisms by default. (2) Integrate unified audit logs for all inter-agent interactions to maintain observability of all agent exchanges. (3) Use interpretability tools to ensure observability of and reasoning behind agent decisions. (4) Require specific information referencing for agents that show where key aspects of their response originated from. Managing third-party components: Verification and management of third-party components can reduce added risk. Recommended best practices: (1) Verify all external third-party components originate from trusted sources and are up to date. (2) Maintain a trusted registry of third-party components. (3) Reference CISA's SBOM guidance when procuring agentic AI systems. (4) Restrict tool use to an approved allow list of tools and versions that are regularly verified as secure. (5) Log agent tool usage and ensure results are captured in system logs in a human-readable format. (6) Establish trigger-action protocols that automatically restrict agent permissions when unexpected behaviour emerges. (7) Codify separation of duties by defining roles such as 'Orchestrator', 'Reader' and 'Actuator' with clear boundaries, consensus mechanisms and delegations expiry. (8) Prohibit agents from modifying their own privileges or initiating unapproved delegation without explicit expiry timers and recorded grant chains. (9) Standardise tool descriptions using a consistent format that avoids persuasive language.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Deploying Agents Securely: Threat Modelling and Governance
text: Best practices — Deploying agents securely (audience: agentic AI vendors and operators). Integrating AI agents into new systems or networks causes significant change in system risk considerations. Threat modelling: Agentic AI can significantly change the threat picture when incorporated into an existing system. Recommended best practices: (1) Perform realistic threat modelling using up-to-date risk taxonomies for agentic AI systems, such as OWASP GenAI Security Project and MITRE ATLAS. (2) Design and implement security controls that address emerging and evolving agent capabilities. (3) Harmonise agentic AI controls with existing security frameworks, national guidance and allied agreements, such as common Zero Trust principles and NIST Zero Trust Architecture guidance. (4) Develop and test incident response procedures to detect, contain and recover from agent compromise. (5) Establish regular third-party reviews of privileged architectures. Governance: Autonomous actions by agentic AI systems introduce new risks, requiring updated governance policies and continuous runtime authentication with centralised policy decision points for each action. Recommended best practices: (1) Implement and maintain governance policies to manage autonomous agents. (2) Define legal accountability and risk ownership for agentic AI systems in policies. (3) Upskill the organisation to build AI literacy. These requirements map directly to ISO 42001 Clause 5 (leadership and commitment) and Clause 6 (planning), which mandate organisational accountability for AI systems.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Deploying Agents Securely: Progressive Deployment, Secure by Default
text: Best practices — Deploying agents securely: Progressive deployment and secure by default. Progressive deployment: The risk profile of AI agents can vary significantly depending on permissions and allowed actions. A progressive approach to deployment aims to limit initial risk until operators and users are more familiar with the limitations of the agentic application. Recommended best practices: (1) Implement phased deployment with progressively increasing access and autonomy, limiting the action space where required — such as restricted APIs or sandboxing. (2) Use graduated autonomy to incrementally increase agent independence whilst maintaining human oversight and understanding. (3) Use continuous evaluation to determine when to expand system scope or when to roll back autonomy and access in response to failures. Secure by default: Safe and secure defaults reduce deployment risk and support system security should degradation occur. Recommended best practices: (1) Set system configurations to fail-safe by default, requiring agents to stop and escalate issues to human reviewers in uncertain scenarios. (2) Use error-handling and failover management to reduce the impact of system failures. (3) Implement graceful degradation models so that agents maintain partial functionality even if some functions fail.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Deploying Agents Securely: Guardrails, Constraints, and Isolation
text: Best practices — Deploying agents securely: Guardrails, constraints and isolation. Guardrails and constraints: Implementing agent guardrails and constraints reduces exposure to many common security risks that AI presents. Recommended best practices: (1) Specify clear, constrained objectives with explicit 'do-not-do' rules. (2) Implement guardrails and hard constraints, such as deny lists and API-level safety policies. (3) Establish declarative safety contracts with constraints and guardrails that agents cannot override. (4) Apply a layered set of guardrail mechanisms, ranging from anomaly detection and rule-based filtering to specialised machine learning algorithms that detect and filter prohibited behaviour. (5) Prioritise review of high-risk incidents, including cases where guardrails are triggered or actions are denied by human reviewers. (6) Deploy a secondary agent to validate new tasks against policy before execution. Isolation: Deployment should consider integration requirements of AI agents and apply isolation where possible to reduce cascading issues should the agent behave unexpectedly or maliciously. Recommended best practices: (1) Implement isolation and segmentation to limit blast radius of agent failure scenarios. (2) Separate high-risk agents into distinct domains. (3) Isolate agents into enclaves with no write access to logs.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Operating Agents Securely: Monitoring and Auditing
text: Best practices — Operating agents securely (audience: agentic AI vendors and operators). Monitoring and auditing: Operators should implement continuous monitoring and auditing to maintain awareness of AI agent operation and ensure traceability for decisions and actions. Continuous auditing processes improve security measures and ensure alignment with governance standards (such as risk management, oversight and usage restrictions). Recommended best practices: (1) Employ monitoring tools that enhance human oversight of agentic AI systems. (2) Monitor all agent operations, including internal processes, not just inputs and outputs. (3) Monitor and log identity and privilege changes and audit regularly for drift, impersonation or misconfiguration. (4) Monitor agent outputs and behaviour for indicators of bias, emerging data drift and other anomalous patterns — including user prompts, tool calls, memory interactions, internal reasoning, decisions made and actions taken. (5) Maintain comprehensive logs and real-time monitoring of live agent behaviour and decision-making. (6) Implement runtime monitoring and anomaly detection using rules or behavioural baselines to identify unusual patterns and trigger alerts or pauses. (7) Establish anomaly detection mechanisms that flag discrepancies between stated intentions and observed behaviours. (8) Use multiple independent monitoring systems that cross-validate agent reports and system logs. (9) Monitor for goal drift by comparing active objectives against approved baseline specifications before execution. (10) Implement auditing practices that combine human review with automated analysis of system logs. (11) Support adaptive defences by using monitoring data to enable rapid responses such as patches based on problems identified in system logs.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Operating Agents Securely: Validate Outputs and Human in the Loop
text: Best practices — Operating agents securely: Validate outputs and human in the loop. Validate outputs: AI agent outputs provide some of the few concrete data points available for monitoring behaviour. Ensuring outputs are valid and reflect desired behaviour is a key measure of correct operation. Recommended best practices: (1) Validate agent outputs by confirming accuracy of critical aspects against multiple sources. (2) Validate agents through cross-checking in environments with redundant agents that validate each other's outputs. (3) Validate tool responses to prevent malicious or unsafe instructions and standardise tool descriptions to avoid persuasive language. Human in the loop: An erroneous or unexpected decision from an agent could result in significant damage, such as deletion of important data. Incorporating human supervision, approval and review into agentic AI workflows is an important control — particularly where actions have high impact or are difficult to reverse. Recommended best practices: (1) Ensure decisions about when human approval is required are determined by system designers or operators, not delegated to the agentic AI system. (2) Prevent agents from autonomously executing high-impact actions or outputs without prior human approval. (3) Insert human-in-the-loop review or approval checkpoints for actions where the cost of error is high — such as system resets, network egress or deletion of critical records. (4) Quarantine requests to delete logs or audit records until reviewed and approved by a human. (5) Clearly assign responsibility and accountability for errors or adverse outcomes caused by the system. (6) Conduct risk assessments to classify agent actions by potential impact, likelihood and reversibility, and apply appropriate safeguards.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Best Practices — Operating Agents Securely: Performance Monitoring and Privileges & Authentication
text: Best practices — Operating agents securely: Performance monitoring and privileges and authentication. Performance monitoring: Degraded or unusual performance could indicate compromise of an agent or component of the agentic system. Recommended best practices: (1) Assess agents' ability to evade security measures, particularly in sensitive or high-impact systems. (2) Conduct regular assessments of an agent's ability to bypass safeguards — such as communication barriers, guardrails, monitors, human-in-the-loop processes and input filters. (3) Use the results from these evaluations to validate existing controls and guide the development of stronger security measures. (4) Limit agent resource usage by applying controls such as rate-limit components to interrupt long-running tasks and disrupt malicious workflows. Privileges and authentication: Ongoing strict privilege management of AI agents is key to long-term security — lapses can change the impact of a buggy agent from minor to catastrophic. Recommended best practices: (1) Limit privileges of AI agents to the minimum required for its task. (2) Restrict scope of privileges to narrowest possible level. (3) Implement agent reputation and trust scoring mechanisms and reduce trust levels when anomalous behaviour is detected. (4) Require just-in-time credentials for high-impact or privileged actions. (5) Authenticate agents with fresh cryptographic proofs before every privileged call. (6) Require cryptographic signing for authorised commands and instructions. (7) Apply cryptographic integrity checks for task definitions and constraints. (8) Require agents to perform cryptographic attestation where agents must prove they are running expected and unmodified code. (9) Continuously verify identity and authorisation at runtime using a centralised policy decision point for each request.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Defend Against Future Risks — Threat Intelligence and Agent-Specific Evaluations
text: Defend against future risks. As agentic AI scales into more roles and gains greater capabilities, organisations must anticipate and address the new risks these systems introduce. Expand threat intelligence through collaboration: Threat intelligence for agentic AI systems is still evolving. Existing frameworks like OWASP 2025 Top 10 Risk & Mitigations for LLMs and Gen AI Apps and MITRE ATLAS focus on LLM vulnerabilities, while some attack vectors unique to agentic AI may not be fully captured. Recommended best practices: (1) Strengthen collaboration between stakeholders to keep pace with evolving threats. (2) Coordinate with major AI developers and government organisations to compile and maintain threat information. (3) Adopt a collaborative security approach such as those described in CISA's AI Cybersecurity Collaboration Playbook. (4) Implement alerting, data collection and tracking methods for malicious actors and techniques. (5) Harmonise threat intelligence across industries to build shared threat taxonomies. Develop robust, agent-specific evaluations: Many existing evaluation methods for agentic AI security are sensitive to minor semantic changes, vary by scenario and only partially capture real-world deployment conditions. Recommended best practices: (1) Develop robust evaluation methods to address the gaps in validating agentic AI systems. (2) Generate benchmark datasets to cover new domains and represent realistic deployment contexts. (3) Use evaluation results to validate emerging security practices and identify failure points. (4) Share evaluation findings to strengthen security assessments and support development of improved security practices across the field.
standard: ASD/ACSC — Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (2026)

title: Defend Against Future Risks — System-Theoretic Approaches and Conclusion
text: Leverage system-theoretic approaches to analyse security: Agentic AI systems are complex ecosystems of LLMs, humans, guardrails, datasets, tools and hardware, where security risks often emerge from interactions between components rather than isolated flaws. Traditional component-level analysis is insufficient. Recommended best practices: (1) Use system-theoretic approaches to analyse agentic AI systems and identify appropriate security measures. (2) Apply System Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) and its security extension STPA-Sec to analyse notional or operational systems, identify security issues, assess mission risk and inform potential mitigations. (3) Use Causal Analysis using System Theory (CAST) to investigate security incidents and identify underlying root causes at the system level. (4) Apply STPA and CAST concurrently across agentic AI system lifecycles. Conclusion: Agentic AI systems offer powerful automation benefits, but their ability to act autonomously across interconnected tools, data and environments introduces security risks that extend beyond those associated with traditional software or GenAI. Privilege escalation, emergent behaviours, structural dependencies and accountability gaps can interact in unpredictable ways. Organisations should approach adoption with security in mind — deploy agentic AI incrementally, beginning with clearly defined low-risk tasks; continuously assess against evolving threat models; treat strong governance, explicit accountability, rigorous monitoring and human oversight as essential prerequisites, not optional safeguards. Prioritise resilience, reversibility and risk containment over efficiency gains.

title: Appendix A — Cyber Security Prerequisites Before Implementation of AI Agents: Design
text: Appendix A — Cyber security prerequisites before implementation of AI agents: Design. Before incorporating AI agents, organisations should establish strong cyber security foundations. Design prerequisites: (1) Implement strong authentication by following Secure by Design principles. (2) Design transparency requirements into the system architecture to enable detection of deception indicators. (3) Use frameworks such as zero trust, the Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) or OAuth2. (4) Build system infrastructure in a secure, sandboxed environment with encryption, rate limiting and sanitisation. (5) Apply the principle of least privilege, assigning only the minimum access required for each role. (6) Limit entitlements to the exact resources, operations and timeframes needed. (7) Replace static, long-lived secrets with ephemeral credentials that expire when the job is complete. (8) Dynamically scope privilege for sub-tasks and revoke elevated rights immediately when finished, mitigating scope creep. (9) Build applications with secure protocols and safe defaults that adhere to communication standards and security policies. (10) Implement message validation by default so that message components include integrity and freshness checks before use.

title: Appendix A — Cyber Security Prerequisites Before Implementation of AI Agents: Development
text: Appendix A — Cyber security prerequisites before implementation of AI agents: Development. Development prerequisites: (1) Apply secure development principles from established DevSecOps frameworks. (2) Minimise application scope and monitor components for unusual or unexpected behaviour. (3) Enforce application understanding — only incorporate components into systems that the owner fully understands and accepts the risks of, including possible external effects and processes that the component may trigger. (4) Refer to frameworks such as the NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) or SLSA Safeguarding artifact integrity for supply chain security. (5) Use supply chain risk management practices for third-party dependencies. (6) Apply existing governance and organisational management policies. (7) Conduct threat modelling using frameworks such as OWASP Top 10:2025, MITRE ATT&CK and MITRE D3FEND, and use the results to inform mitigations tailored to the operational environment. (8) Plan and regularly test incident response plans and teams. Relationship to ISO 42001: These prerequisites directly support ISO 42001 Clause 8.4 (AI system lifecycle processes) and Clause 8.5 (AI system impact assessment), requiring organisations to embed security requirements into the full lifecycle before agentic AI is deployed in any operational context.
